title: People Now Spend 14.5% of Their Lives in Poor Health
paragraphs: People around the world are living longer than ever before. However, according to a major new global study, they are also spending more of their lives in poor health.

The study was carried out by the Institute for Health Metrics and Evaluation (IHME) at the University of Washington as part of the Global Burden of Disease study, a large project that tracks health around the world. It was published in the journal The Lancet Public Health in July 2026 and looked at data from 1990 to 2023.

The researchers found that global life expectancy at birth rose from 64.6 years in 1990 to 73.8 years in 2023. However, healthy life expectancy, meaning the number of years people can expect to live in good health, rose more slowly, from 55.9 to 63.1 years. As a result, the average number of years that people spend in poor health increased from 8.8 years to 10.7 years. In other words, the share of life spent in poor health rose from 13.6% to 14.5%. This gap widened in almost every country studied.

The gap was largest in wealthy regions. In 2023, the United States had the biggest gap of any country, at 14 years, followed by Australia, at 13.9 years, and Canada, at 13.7 years. In contrast, the gap was smallest in sub-Saharan Africa, at 9.0 years.

The study also found important differences between men and women. Although women live longer than men in every region of the world, they also spend more years in poor health. In 2023, women spent an average of 12.1 years in poor health, compared with 9.3 years for men.

Most of these unhealthy years are caused by long-term conditions that are not usually fatal. The biggest contributors were problems affecting the muscles and bones, particularly low back pain, followed by mental health conditions such as depression and anxiety, age-related hearing loss and injuries from falls.

According to Dr. Christopher Murray, the director of IHME, progress in healthy aging should be measured not only by lifespan, but also by healthspan. The researchers have called for more investment in prevention, rehabilitation, mental health services and the management of long-term conditions.
